newsitem.title: CONGO: France wraps up Congo evacuations as bullets fly.
newsitem.headline: France wraps up Congo evacuations as bullets fly.

text.p: France wrapped up its airlift of foreign nationals from the Congo Republic capital of Brazzaville during a brief lull in fighting on Sunday and prepared to pull its forces out of the city.

Paris said the 1,200 or so force, which has evacuated well over 5,000 French and foreign nationals, would start pulling out of the oil-producing former French colony from Monday, despite calls from President Pascal Lissouba and others for it to stay.

Earlier, envoys of Lissouba and former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso, whose rival supporters have been at the heart of over a week of bloody ethnic and political fighting, left the city for peace talks in Gabon.
"All the French nationals who wanted to go are gone and the bulk of the foreigners as well," French military spokesman Colonel Henry Pelissier said. "Our mission is accomplished."
France said its embassy would stay open with appropriate security. "We start pulling out in principle on Monday and that will take something less than a week," Pelissier said.
Two evacuation flights left on Sunday after militia loyal to Sassou Nguesso fired mortar bombs and tank shells at government loyalists at the airport.
The barrage and crackling gunfire, which started at 2 a.m. and lasted for much of the day, followed two days of relative calm in the city, where bodies litter the streets.
The last plane spent barely 10 minutes on the ground.
Armed French soldiers in flak jackets and helmets guarded the final 87 evacuees, many of them African children who were led through the dust kicked up by the rotating propellers.
Bullets flew overhead shortly before the plane landed and firing broke out again after it had left.
Sixteen French evacuees were bound for Gabon, the rest, mostly Africans, for the Congolese port of Pointe Noire.
The conflict started on June 5 after the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised arms in the runup to a July 27 election.
Sunday's exchanges followed two days of relative calm in the city after the two sides declared a truce on Wednesday.
Militia loyal to Sassou Nguesso advanced on the airport on Sunday and bombarded troops loyal to Lissouba there, saying they wanted to take out guns that shelled their northern stronghold.
Lissouba called on Sunday for French troops to stay.

"I am making a fervent call. I would have liked French forces, with ourselves and those in the positions opposite us to have formed a buffer force, to avoid exactly what is going on today," he told French television.

He told Radio France International the election must take place as planned and called there for an African peace force to oversee polling. "These elections must take place," he said. "Democracy cannot be negotiated."
Sassou Nguesso did not rule out the idea of an outside force. "The international community must organise the elections, check them and ensure security," he told the same radio station.
Mediators say Gabon's veteran President Omar Bongo will host peace talks on Monday in his capital Libreville.
French Ambassador Raymond Cesaire played down Sunday's fighting. "These things happen during negotiations when sides try to improve their positions," he said.

Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas, whose supporters were in the thick of bloody clashes that killed 2,000 people after a disputed 1993 parliamentary poll, has been a key mediator. His militia have stayed out of the fighting this time.
The smell of rotting bodies permeates parts of the city. Some sources say the death toll could run into hundreds and maybe even several thousand. Many dead lie where they fell.
"The number of bodies in the morgue is uncountable," surgeon Kibongo Nazerne said at the main University Hospital Centre. "It has space for 140 bodies but there are many more than that."
Pope John Paul, addressing pilgrims at the Vatican on Sunday, condemned the fighting and urged reconciliation.
